transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I just don’t feel like doing any of the things I used to love—my workshop, church, even fishing don’t mean anything to me right now. It feels like I've just completely lost my drive for everything that used to make me happy.
How long have you been feeling this way, and was it a gradual change or did it start suddenly after something specific happened?

These feelings really took hold over the last three weeks, starting right after my doctor raised concerns about my memory and ordered some cognitive testing. He told me to cut back on driving and other independent activities, which felt like a massive blow to my independence and who I am.
Have you experienced any feelings of guilt, worthlessness, or self-blame alongside the loss of interest in activities you once enjoyed?

I wouldn't say I feel guilty, but I do feel incredibly useless lately because of this constant mental fog. Not being able to handle simple tasks has completely shaken my self-reliance and my identity as an engineer and mentor. It’s hard to feel any worth when you can't even trust your own mind anymore.
Can you tell me if you've experienced any thoughts of death or suicidal ideation since you started feeling this way, or have your feelings been more about a loss of purpose and identity?

To be honest, it's a mix of both; at night when it's quiet, I find myself thinking it might be easier if I just didn’t wake up so my wife wouldn't have to watch me fall apart, though I don't have any plan to harm myself. It all ties back to losing my sense of purpose, because without my identity as an engineer and a mentor, I feel completely lost.
Can you describe how often these feelings of uselessness and thoughts about not waking up occur, and are they constant or do they vary throughout the day?

The feeling of being useless is there pretty much all day, especially when the brain fog rolls in and I can't even make a simple decision. But those thoughts about not waking up really take over at night when the house gets quiet. That's when I lie there, just dreading the thought of my wife having to watch me fall apart like this.
Have you had any periods in the past where you felt similar to how you're feeling now, or is this the first time you've experienced such a significant loss of interest and feelings of uselessness?

No, I have never felt anything like this before in my life. I've always been a very active, self-reliant person, so this overwhelming feeling of uselessness and losing interest in everything is completely new and honestly quite scary. It all just started recently after my doctor brought up those concerns about my memory.
Would you say that these feelings of uselessness and loss of interest in activities are present most of the day, every day, or are there some days where you feel slightly better or more engaged?

It's pretty much every single day, most of the day, with no real breaks. For the last three weeks, it has felt like a constant, heavy cloud over me, and there really aren't any 'good' days. Even when my wife or friends try to get me involved, I just can't bring myself to care or feel any different.
Can you think of any activities, no matter how small, that you still find some pleasure in or look forward to, even if it's just for a brief moment?

Honestly, there isn't anything right now that brings me any pleasure or excitement. I'll look right at my fishing rods or my toolbox and just feel completely blank, like the color has been turned down on everything. Without any drive or curiosity left, I usually just make an excuse and stay in my chair.

You've mentioned feeling useless and having thoughts about not waking up, but can you tell me if you've experienced any significant changes in your appetite or sleep patterns over the last three weeks?

My appetite has really dropped off lately, and I usually just get by on a cup of coffee and some toast because food doesn't appeal to me and fixing a meal feels like too much effort. As for my sleep, that hasn't really changed much or been the main issue.
Have you noticed any slowing down in your physical movements or speech over the past three weeks, or do you feel like you're moving and reacting at about the same pace as before?

Yes, I've slowed down significantly over the last three weeks, and my wife constantly asks if I'm sick because I move so slowly and take forever just to get dressed. I often find myself shuffling around the house or just sitting at the kitchen table, staring at the salt shaker for ten minutes before I even realize I haven't moved. It's incredibly frustrating how sluggish my body feels now.
Can you describe a typical day in terms of your motivation and energy levels, and how that compares to your normal self before these feelings started?

Before this, I was always active, running household projects, mentoring kids at the maker space, and planning fishing trips. Now, a typical day is spent just sitting in my chair, shuffling around, and relying on my wife to remind me to do basic chores. It's incredibly frustrating to go from being so productive to barely managing to get out of my seat.
Can you elaborate more on what you mean by 'slowing down' and if this feeling of sluggishness is affecting your ability to initiate or complete tasks throughout the day?

It’s like my body is stuck in slow motion, and my wife constantly points out how I shuffle around and take forever just to get dressed. I'll get completely stuck staring at something simple, like the salt shaker on the table, for ten minutes without even realizing it. This heavy sluggishness makes it incredibly hard to start or finish basic chores, leaving me relying on my wife to handle almost everything.
Have you experienced any unusual thoughts, such as hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there, since you started feeling this way?
No, I haven't experienced anything like that at all. While my mind feels incredibly foggy and I'm deeply depressed, I've never heard voices or seen things that aren't actually there.

You mentioned a lot of changes in your mood and motivation, but can you tell me if you've noticed any differences in your thinking, such as having thoughts that don't seem to make sense or feeling like your thoughts are being controlled by something outside of yourself?
No, I haven't experienced anything like that. My mind just feels incredibly foggy and slow lately, but it's definitely my own thoughts and not controlled by anything outside of myself.

Do you ever experience any improvement in your mood or interest in activities in response to positive events or interactions with loved ones, or does your low mood remain consistent regardless of what's happening around you?

No, my low mood and lack of interest are completely constant and never seem to improve. Even when my wife tries to encourage me by reminding me about my friends from church or the kids at the maker space who care about me, I just feel completely numb and empty inside. I simply can't find any joy or excitement, no matter what is happening around me.
Can you describe how your slowed physical movements and sluggishness have affected your daily activities and interactions with others over the past three weeks?

For the last three weeks, I've been moving incredibly slowly, shuffling around and taking forever to get dressed, or just staring blankly at a salt shaker on the table. This sluggishness makes it hard to manage even basic chores, which has really strained things with my wife because she constantly asks if I'm sick and now has to remind me to do almost everything.

You've mentioned feeling mentally foggy, but can you clarify if this foginess includes any disorganized thinking or if your thoughts feel coherent to you, even if they are negative or preoccupied with feelings of uselessness?

My thoughts are coherent rather than chaotic, but they feel incredibly slow, muddy, and easy to lose track of. I constantly lose my train of thought mid-sentence and struggle with simple decisions like what shirt to wear, which all blends into a frustrating, foggy blur. Mostly, my mind is just heavily preoccupied with feeling useless and worrying that I'm losing my mental sharpness.

Can you describe in more detail how your doctor's concerns about your memory and the subsequent cognitive testing have affected your perception of yourself and your abilities, and do you think this is a major contributor to your current feelings of uselessness and loss of interest in activities?

Yes, being told to cut back on driving and hearing those memory concerns felt like a direct blow to my self-reliance and my identity as an engineer and mentor. It is absolutely the main trigger for my current state, because it made me fixate constantly on the terrifying fear that I'm losing my mind. That fear is exactly what caused me to pull away from my workshop, church, and everything else over the last three weeks.

Do you think your feelings of uselessness and loss of interest would improve if your memory concerns were addressed or if you found ways to adapt to your current cognitive challenges, or are these feelings more deeply tied to a fear of losing your identity and independence?

The memory lapses themselves are frustrating, but the core of the issue is definitely the deep fear of losing my identity and independence. Being told to cut back on driving and mentoring felt like a direct blow to who I am as an engineer and a community figure. That is what makes me feel so useless and makes even my favorite hobbies feel completely pointless now.

Do you believe that if your cognitive functions and memory were to improve or stabilize, your interest in activities and sense of purpose would also return, or do you think your current state of mind is more influenced by the emotional impact of losing your independence and identity?

It’s a mix of both, but the loss of my independence and identity has hit me much deeper than the memory lapses themselves. The fear of fading away upstairs makes me wonder what the point of anything is, especially since losing my role as a self-reliant engineer, mentor, and driver has stripped away my sense of usefulness. Even if my memory stabilized tomorrow, I feel like the damage to my confidence and who I am has already been done.

Do you think your current feelings of uselessness and loss of interest in activities would significantly change if you were able to find new ways to adapt to your cognitive challenges and maintain some level of independence, or are these feelings now deeply ingrained regardless of potential adaptations?

Right now, it feels incredibly hard to even imagine adapting. Because I feel like I'm just fading away upstairs in this foggy, frustrating blur, the loss of my self-reliance and engineering identity feels absolute. At this moment, these feelings of uselessness are so deeply ingrained that I just can't see how any adaptation could ever bring back who I used to be.

Do you think your feelings of uselessness and loss of interest would diminish if you were able to find meaningful ways to contribute or engage in activities that don't rely heavily on the cognitive functions you're concerned about, such as your memory?

It's hard to imagine finding meaning in simpler activities when my entire identity was built on being an engineer, a mentor, and someone who solves complex problems. With this constant mental fog and the complete lack of interest I feel right now, even trying to think of alternatives just feels exhausting and pointless.

Do you think your current feelings of depression and loss of interest would be significantly alleviated if your cognitive decline were to slow down or stabilize, or are these feelings more closely tied to the emotional impact of your diagnosis and perceived loss of identity?

These feelings are definitely more tied to the emotional blow of losing my independence and identity. Being told to cut back on driving and mentoring felt like a direct challenge to my self-reliance as an engineer and community member. It's the terrifying fear of "fading away upstairs" and becoming useless that drives this heavy feeling, much more than the cognitive symptoms themselves.

Do you think your feelings of depression and loss of interest would return to normal if your memory concerns and cognitive decline were completely addressed, or have these feelings become a separate issue for you?

While those memory worries and losing my driving privileges definitely started all of this, the depression has really become a separate, overwhelming weight of its own. Even if my memory were completely fine tomorrow, this heavy, hollow ache in my chest and the feeling of being useless are so deep now that I don't think I could just bounce back. It really feels like its own separate beast at this point.

Do you believe that your current depressive symptoms would improve if you were able to find ways to cope with or adapt to your cognitive decline, or do you think they have become independent of your concerns about memory and cognitive function?

They are completely tied together, because my entire identity was built on my mind, problem-solving, and my independence. It feels impossible to "adapt" to the idea of losing my mind, which is why everything feels so hopeless and pointless right now. This heavy, hollow feeling started the exact moment the doctor raised those cognitive concerns, and I just can't separate them.

Do you think there's a possibility that addressing your depressive symptoms first could help you better cope with your cognitive decline, or do you believe that your cognitive decline must be addressed before you can make any progress with your depression?

I understand your point, but to me, the fear of losing my mind feels like the absolute root of everything, and these dark feelings only started after the doctor raised those concerns about my memory. It is hard to imagine finding hope or making progress with my mood while I still feel like I'm fading away upstairs and losing my independence. That being said, I am completely exhausted by all of this and am very open to any help you can offer.

You've mentioned a complete loss of interest in activities you once enjoyed, but can you think of any situations or contexts where you might still experience some pleasure or interest, even if it's very slight or fleeting?

No, I really can't think of any situations where that happens. Even when I try to search my mind for something that might bring a little joy, there really aren't any moments, however fleeting, where I feel any spark of interest or pleasure lately. Everything just feels completely flat.
If you were to experience significant improvement in your depressive symptoms, do you think your concerns about cognitive decline and loss of identity would still be as distressing to you?

Honestly, it's very hard to even imagine feeling better right now, so I'm really not sure if those worries would go away. The fear of losing my mind and my independence feels like a very real, separate reality rather than just a symptom of being down. I just don't know if feeling less depressed would make those fears disappear.

Do you think that if your depressive symptoms were effectively managed, you would still be distressed by your cognitive decline, or would addressing your depression significantly reduce your concerns about losing your independence and identity?

Right now, the depression and my fear of cognitive decline feel deeply tangled together. Because my entire identity has been built on being a self-reliant engineer and mentor, the actual threat of losing my mental sharpness and independence would still be incredibly distressing even if my mood improved. That said, the depression and this constant fog definitely make everything feel much more hopeless and hard to parse right now.

Do you think your current feelings of depression and loss of interest would be significantly alleviated if you received a definitive diagnosis regarding your cognitive decline, such as a diagnosis of a specific dementia or a reassurance that your cognitive decline is not progressing?

The uncertainty and constant fear of "losing my mind" are a massive part of what is weighing me down right now. While reassurance that I'm not progressing would be a huge relief and might help me regain some hope, I am also terrified that a definitive diagnosis of dementia would make me feel even more hopeless and useless. It would just confirm my worst fear of "fading away upstairs" and completely losing my independence.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of persistent and profound loss of interest in activities, feelings of worthlessness, significant weight loss (due to decreased appetite), and recurrent thoughts of death, which have been present for more than two weeks, align with the diagnostic criteria for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD).
